**Syntax and values.** Start with the formal syntax on the MDN reference page. In production, prefer a valid baseline value, then add a modern value only when it improves the experience. Common value families include keywords, lengths, percentages, colors, custom-identifiers, functions, and global keywords such as `inherit`, `initial`, `unset`, `revert`, and `revert-layer`.

**Practical guidance.** Use `border-inline-end-color` where its behavior is part of the component design. Keep the declaration close to the selector that owns it, use a custom property when consumers need a supported token, and avoid coupling the rule to a fragile DOM depth. Check computed styles when debugging because the authored declaration may be overridden, inherited, or invalid after variable substitution. The snippets below use a concrete baseline plus a tokenized form so they remain useful when copied into a real stylesheet.

**Fallback and compatibility.** Treat the feature as progressive enhancement if it is new, experimental, vendor-prefixed, or dependent on a newer value grammar. Put the baseline first, use `@supports` for meaningful capability detection, and verify the exact target browsers with Can I Use and MDN compatibility data. Do not claim that a syntax transform reproduces a browser layout algorithm.

**Accessibility and performance.** Confirm that the declaration does not hide focus, clip essential content, reduce contrast, disable zoom, or create motion that ignores user preferences. If `border-inline-end-color` is read or written through CSSOM, batch reads and writes and validate any external input.

**Example: Minimal declaration.**

```css
.component { border-inline-end-color: initial; }
```

**Example: Component token.**

```css
:root {
  --book-border-inline-end-color: initial;
}
.component {
  border-inline-end-color: var(--book-border-inline-end-color, initial);
}
```

**Example: Progressive enhancement.**

```css
.component {
  border-inline-end-color: initial;
}

@supports (border-inline-end-color: initial) {
  .component { border-inline-end-color: var(--book-border-inline-end-color, initial); }
}
```

### `font`

**Role.** This property affects font selection, text shaping, line breaking, or inline formatting. The `font` property is commonly used when a component needs an explicit, inspectable contract instead of relying on browser defaults.

**Syntax and values.** Start with the formal syntax on the MDN reference page. In production, prefer a valid baseline value, then add a modern value only when it improves the experience. Common value families include keywords, lengths, percentages, colors, custom-identifiers, functions, and global keywords such as `inherit`, `initial`, `unset`, `revert`, and `revert-layer`.

**Practical guidance.** Use `font` where its behavior is part of the component design. Keep the declaration close to the selector that owns it, use a custom property when consumers need a supported token, and avoid coupling the rule to a fragile DOM depth. Check computed styles when debugging because the authored declaration may be overridden, inherited, or invalid after variable substitution. The snippets below use a concrete baseline plus a tokenized form so they remain useful when copied into a real stylesheet.

**Fallback and compatibility.** Treat the feature as progressive enhancement if it is new, experimental, vendor-prefixed, or dependent on a newer value grammar. Put the baseline first, use `@supports` for meaningful capability detection, and verify the exact target browsers with Can I Use and MDN compatibility data. Do not claim that a syntax transform reproduces a browser layout algorithm.

**Accessibility and performance.** Confirm that the declaration does not hide focus, clip essential content, reduce contrast, disable zoom, or create motion that ignores user preferences. If `font` is read or written through CSSOM, batch reads and writes and validate any external input.

**Example: Minimal declaration.**

```css
.copy { font: var(--font, normal); }
```

**Example: Component token.**

```css
:root {
  --book-font: initial;
}
.component {
  font: var(--book-font, initial);
}
```

**Example: Progressive enhancement.**

```css
.component {
  font: initial;
}

@supports (font: initial) {
  .component { font: var(--book-font, initial); }
}
```

**Related concepts.** See the surrounding entries for neighboring longhands and shorthands, and review the `Typography and text` chapter before changing a component-wide contract.

### `perspective`

**Role.** This property participates in animation, transitions, transforms, motion paths, or view timelines. The `perspective` property is commonly used when a component needs an explicit, inspectable contract instead of relying on browser defaults.

**Syntax and values.** Start with the formal syntax on the MDN reference page. In production, prefer a valid baseline value, then add a modern value only when it improves the experience. Common value families include keywords, lengths, percentages, colors, custom-identifiers, functions, and global keywords such as `inherit`, `initial`, `unset`, `revert`, and `revert-layer`.

**Practical guidance.** Use `perspective` where its behavior is part of the component design. Keep the declaration close to the selector that owns it, use a custom property when consumers need a supported token, and avoid coupling the rule to a fragile DOM depth. ## Appendix A: Browser-support snapshot policy

This edition records a browser-support methodology rather than pretending that a printed book can remain current forever. At the time of editing, check the latest three versions of these ten desktop/mobile channels: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari, Chrome Android, Safari iOS, Samsung Internet, Opera, UC Browser, and Android Browser. Record exact versions and the date of the check in the release notes. Use feature-level tables, not a single â€œCSS supportedâ€ score.

For a print edition, place a QR code beside this appendix that points to a maintained compatibility page. The print book should teach the decision process; the web page should carry the moving numbers.

### Can I Use: live browser compatibility

Use [Can I Use](https://caniuse.com/) to inspect feature-level support across current desktop and mobile browser versions. Search for the exact feature, read the notes for partial support and implementation caveats, and record the date of your review. The result is a decision aid, not a permanent guarantee.

![QR code linking to Can I Use](/qr/caniuse.png)

Scan to open [Can I Use](https://caniuse.com/).

Direct link: [https://caniuse.com/](https://caniuse.com/)

When using the printed book, scan the QR code for current data. When reviewing a web feature, also compare the relevant MDN compatibility notes and test the actual browsers, devices, and assistive technologies that matter to your audience.

## Appendix B: Submission package for publishers

This appendix is for producing a personal spiral-bound print edition, not for submitting a traditional publishing proposal. For one copy or a small private run, the most practical route is to prepare a print-ready PDF and submit it to a local print shop or an online book printer that offers coil binding.

### Recommended options

| Option | Best for | What to submit |
|---|---|---|
| Local independent print shop | Highest control over paper, covers, proofing, and binding | Print-ready PDF and a written specification |
| FedEx Office | Convenient upload, local pickup, and standard document sizes | PDF; choose coil binding and cover options where available |
| Staples Print & Marketing | Local document printing and coil binding where the selected store supports it | PDF; confirm binding capacity and turnaround first |
| Lulu personal printing | A book-like upload workflow with paperback coil-bound options | Interior PDF, cover PDF, trim size, paper, and binding selection |
| University or library print center | Cost-conscious personal copies and large technical documents | PDF plus page-count and binding instructions |

Service availability, page limits, paper stocks, and local turnaround can change. Confirm the exact binding option and maximum page count before placing the order. For a personal spiral edition, local shops are often the easiest place to inspect a proof and request changes.

### Metal ring binding: Wire-O or twin-loop wire

Yes. Ask for **Wire-O**, **twin-loop wire**, **double-loop wire**, **double-O**, or **ring-wire binding**. This is the metal-ring option: pages and covers are punched, then a preformed metal wire is closed through the holes. It lies flat and can usually fold back on itself, making it a strong choice for a technical reference used beside a computer.

Wire-O is different from a continuous plastic spiral coil:

| Binding | Material and shape | Strengths | Tradeoffs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plastic coil | Continuous plastic helix | Flexible, economical, easy to turn | Less formal appearance; coil can deform if handled roughly |
| Wire-O | Preformed metal double loops | Professional appearance, lies flat, folds back | Printer must have the correct punch and wire size; pages are not easily removable |
| Three-ring binder | Separate metal rings in a cover | Pages can be added or removed | Bulky, pages can shift, and the spine is wider |

For this book, I would request black or silver Wire-O with a clear front cover and opaque back cover. Ask the printer whether it supports 2:1 or 3:1 hole spacing, the maximum thickness, and the binding-side margin. Do not assume that a shop offering plastic coil also offers metal Wire-O.

The PDF should reserve extra space on the punched edge. A printer may recommend approximately 0.75â€“0.875 inches, but use the shopâ€™s template because the required margin depends on paper thickness, punch pattern, and wire size. [Wire-O guidance from PrintingCenterUSA](https://www.printingcenterusa.com/help-center/knowledge-base/binding-wire-o/) describes a 7/8-inch binding-side margin, while other binders use different specifications.

### My practical recommendation

Start with one proof at a local print shop. Request:

- US Letter or A4, depending on where you will read it;
- double-sided printing;
- a clear front cover and durable back cover;
- black plastic coil binding;
- 28â€“32 lb interior paper for a long reference book;
- heavier cover stock or laminated covers;
- color printing only for diagrams, QR codes, and pages where color carries meaning.

If the proof is satisfactory and you want a second copy, compare its total price with Luluâ€™s personal-printing workflow. A local shop is usually better for immediate feedback; an online printer is more convenient when you want repeatable copies shipped to you.

### Prepare the print-ready PDF

Do not submit the SvelteKit HTML or the raw Markdown file to a print shop. Export a paginated PDF with:

1. A defined trim size and page orientation.
2. Embedded fonts.
3. Page numbers and a tested table of contents.
4. A title page, edition date, and copyright page.
5. Headers, footers, and chapter openers that do not collide with the binding edge.
6. Print-safe contrast and code blocks that do not rely on a dark screen theme alone.
7. Images and QR codes at sufficient resolution.
8. Intentional blank pages where chapters need to begin on a right-hand page.
9. A front cover PDF and a separate interior PDF if the service requests them separately.

For coil binding, leave a generous inner margin on the punched edge. Luluâ€™s formatting guidance recommends additional binding-side space for coil-bound books; a local printer may use a different punch and margin specification, so ask the printer for its exact template before final export.

### Suggested file package

```text
css-definitive-reference/
â”œâ”€â”€ CSS-Definitive-Reference-interior.pdf
â”œâ”€â”€ CSS-Definitive-Reference-cover.pdf
â”œâ”€â”€ CSS-Definitive-Reference-proof-notes.md
â””â”€â”€ CSS-Definitive-Reference-source.md
```

The Markdown file is useful for revisions, but the PDF is the file that controls pagination and print output. Keep the source and print proof together so a later compatibility update can be traced to the edition that was printed.

### Recommended fonts for the print edition

Use three clearly separated typographic roles: a readable text face, a sturdy display face, and a monospace face for code. The web edition already uses this three-role model; the print edition should preserve the roles while using embedded, print-tested font files.

| Role | Primary recommendation | Good alternative | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Body text | Source Serif 4 | Literata or Charter | Paragraphs, notes, captions, and long explanations |
| Headings and interface labels | DM Sans | Source Sans 3 or IBM Plex Sans | Chapter titles, headings, tables, badges, and navigation |
| Code | DM Mono | Source Code Pro or IBM Plex Mono | CSS, JavaScript, URLs, commands, and tokens |

The recommended combination for this book is Source Serif 4 for reading text, DM Sans for headings and interface labels, and DM Mono for code. It creates a clear contrast between explanation and implementation while remaining familiar to readers who spend long periods reading technical material.

```css
:root {
  --font-reading: "Source Serif 4", Georgia, serif;
  --font-display: "DM Sans", "Source Sans 3", Arial, sans-serif;
  --font-code: "DM Mono", "Source Code Pro", "SFMono-Regular", Consolas, monospace;
}

body { font-family: var(--font-reading); }
h1, h2, h3, h4, nav, .badge, .button { font-family: var(--font-display); }
code, pre, kbd, samp { font-family: var(--font-code); }
```

For a print PDF, embed the exact font files and confirm that the licenses permit embedding and distribution. Open-source families from Google Fonts are convenient, but still keep a copy of the license and record the font version used for the edition.

### Print typography checks

Before approving the proof:

1. Check body text at approximately 10.5â€“11.5 pt with 1.35â€“1.55 line spacing.
2. Keep the prose measure near 55â€“75 characters per line.
3. Confirm that headings do not orphan at the bottom of a page.
4. Check that code remains legible at approximately 8.5â€“9.5 pt.
5. Inspect similar glyphs such as `0/O`, `1/l/I`, braces, brackets, and punctuation.
6. Verify that code lines wrap intentionally or are split into readable examples.
7. Compare the font metrics against the HTML edition before final pagination.
8. Print a grayscale proof; hierarchy should remain clear without color.

Changing fonts after pagination can alter line breaks, page count, table widths, code wrapping, and the position of QR codes. Treat the font choice as part of the print specification, not as a final cosmetic adjustment.

### Print-shop submission note

Use a short specification instead of sending an open-ended request:

```text
Please print one double-sided, full-color proof from the attached PDF.
Trim size: US Letter, portrait.
Binding: black or silver Wire-O / twin-loop metal wire, left edge.
Covers: clear front cover and heavy opaque back cover.
Interior: 28â€“32 lb white paper.
Please confirm the binding-side margin, hole pattern, wire size, and maximum page count before production.
Please provide a proof or digital preflight for approval.
```

### Copyright and personal-use boundary

This workflow assumes that you own or have permission to print the manuscript, code, illustrations, fonts, and other included assets. A personal copy of your own book is different from uploading someone elseâ€™s copyrighted book to a print service. Check licenses for fonts, screenshots, third-party code, and logos before ordering copies.

## Appendix C: Can I Email

Web CSS compatibility and email CSS compatibility are different problem spaces. Email clients may remove `<style>` blocks, rewrite markup, limit selectors, ignore modern layout systems, or render HTML through engines with very different capabilities. Before shipping a campaign, template, or transactional message, check the exact HTML and CSS feature in [Can I Email](https://www.caniemail.com/).

### Can I Email: live email-client compatibility

Use [Can I Email](https://www.caniemail.com/) to check HTML and CSS support across email clients. Scan the QR code in the print edition or use the direct link below to open the current feature tables.

![QR code linking to Can I Email](/qr/caniemail.png)

Direct link: [https://www.caniemail.com/](https://www.caniemail.com/)

### What Can I Email provides

Can I Email is a feature-support reference for HTML and CSS in email clients. Its tables cover client-specific behavior across desktop, mobile, and webmail environments, including Apple Mail, Gmail, Outlook, Yahoo Mail, Samsung Email, Thunderbird, Proton Mail, and others. Use it alongside your own inbox tests and delivery platform documentation; it is a compatibility reference, not a guarantee that a particular template will render identically.

- Can I Email home: https://www.caniemail.com/
- Estimated support methodology: https://www.caniemail.com/support/
- Feature directory: https://www.caniemail.com/features/

### Email-safe baseline

Start with a resilient baseline: table-based structure where necessary, inline styles for critical declarations, explicit dimensions for important assets, descriptive alternative text, a readable fallback font stack, and a plain-text alternative. Add modern enhancements only when the message remains useful without them.

```html
<table role="presentation" width="100%" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0" border="0">
  <tr>
    <td style="padding: 24px; font-family: Arial, sans-serif; color: #172033;">
      <h1 style="margin: 0 0 12px; font-size: 28px; line-height: 1.2;">
        A resilient email heading
      </h1>
      <p style="margin: 0; font-size: 16px; line-height: 1.5;">
        The message remains useful when advanced CSS is unavailable.
      </p>
    </td>
  </tr>
</table>
```

### A practical compatibility workflow

1. Identify the feature: for example, `display: grid`, `position: sticky`, `background-image`, `border-radius`, or a media query.
2. Search for the feature on Can I Email and inspect the client-specific notes, not only the headline percentage.
3. Define the fallback first. A single-column layout is often a better email fallback than attempting to simulate a full web layout.
4. Add the enhancement behind a safe condition or in a way that degrades harmlessly.
5. Test representative clients, including the clients that matter to your audience, and inspect both visual output and accessible reading order.

```css
/* Baseline: readable in a simple email renderer. */
.email-columns {
  display: block;
}

/* Enhancement: clients that support the feature can use two columns. */
@media screen and (min-width: 600px) {
  .email-columns {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr;
    gap: 24px;
  }
}
```

### How this appendix fits the book

Use Can I Use for browser compatibility and Can I Email for email-client compatibility. Do not transfer a browser support result directly into an email template decision. When a feature is unavailable, prefer a useful baseline, a progressive enhancement, and a documented test result over a fragile workaround.

## Appendix D: Vendor-prefixed CSS properties

Vendor prefixes are historical compatibility markers such as `-webkit-`, `-moz-`, `-ms-`, and `-o-`. Browsers used them to expose experimental or non-standard behavior before a feature was standardized. New CSS features generally ship unprefixed now, so a prefix should not be added automatically and should never be used as a substitute for checking current browser support.

The table below records prefixed properties that can still appear in production stylesheets or legacy code. It is intentionally selective: it focuses on properties a maintainer may need to recognize, migrate, or retain for a documented target rather than listing every historical engine extension.

| Standard or related property | Prefixed form | Current guidance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `appearance` | `-webkit-appearance`, `-moz-appearance` | Put the standard property first. Keep a prefixed declaration only when testing shows that a specific legacy control-rendering target requires it. |
| `backdrop-filter` | `-webkit-backdrop-filter` | Use the unprefixed declaration first, then the WebKit fallback when supporting older Safari versions. Always provide an opaque or translucent background fallback. |
| `text-size-adjust` | `-webkit-text-size-adjust` | Use the standard property first and the prefixed alias only for older mobile WebKit behavior. Avoid disabling text adjustment unless the responsive layout has been tested carefully. |
| `mask-*` | `-webkit-mask-*` | Treat prefixed mask declarations as a targeted Safari compatibility layer. Keep a non-mask fallback when the effect is decorative or affects contrast. |
| `text-stroke` | `-webkit-text-stroke`, `-webkit-text-stroke-width`, `-webkit-text-stroke-color` | This remains a WebKit extension rather than a broadly standardized property. Use it only as a progressive visual enhancement and preserve readable filled text beneath it. |
| â€” | `-webkit-tap-highlight-color` | WebKit/Blink mobile UI extension. Use sparingly; do not remove the tap indication without supplying another visible pressed or focus state. |
| â€” | `-webkit-touch-callout` | WebKit interaction extension. Avoid relying on it for functionality; it only changes a platform gesture affordance. |
| â€” | `-webkit-box-reflect` | Non-standard visual reflection. Do not use it for essential content or layout. |

### The standard-first declaration pattern

When a prefixed declaration is genuinely required, place the unprefixed declaration first and the prefixed form immediately after it. The later declaration can override the standard one in an older engine without hiding the intended standard behavior from current browsers.

```css
.glass-panel {
  background: rgb(255 255 255 / .72);
  backdrop-filter: blur(1rem);
  -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(1rem);
}
```

Do not copy this pattern blindly. Verify the exact target browsers, test the fallback, and remove the prefix when it no longer serves a supported audience.

### Feature-querying a prefixed fallback

If the enhancement is optional, feature-query both the standard and prefixed forms. The condition should describe the capability the component needs, not the brand of the browser.

```css
.surface {
  background: #f4f7fb;
}

@supports (backdrop-filter: blur(1rem)) or
          (-webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(1rem)) {
  .surface {
    background: rgb(244 247 251 / .72);
    backdrop-filter: blur(1rem);
    -webkit-backdrop-filter: blur(1rem);
  }
}
```

The fallback remains useful when neither declaration is supported. A feature query does not make a non-standard property standard; it only prevents unsupported syntax from becoming part of the active enhancement path.

### Migrating legacy prefixed code

When reviewing an older stylesheet:

1. Search for each prefix and group declarations by the feature they implement.
2. Check whether an unprefixed standard property now covers the use case.
3. Put the standard declaration first and retain a prefix only with a documented browser requirement.
4. Replace prefixed selectors and pseudo-elements with standard equivalents when available, such as `::file-selector-button` or `::placeholder`.
5. Test visual behavior, keyboard focus, touch feedback, and reduced-motion or high-contrast modes.
6. Remove the compatibility line after the support policy no longer includes the affected browser.

```css
/* Legacy stylesheet: migrate toward the standard property. */
.control {
  -webkit-appearance: none;
  appearance: none;
}

/* Keep the native focus signal visible after changing appearance. */
.control:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid currentColor;
  outline-offset: 2px;
}
```

Changing `appearance` can remove important platform affordances. Rebuild the control's focus, disabled, invalid, and pressed states before shipping a custom appearance.

### What not to do

Do not write a long list of every historical prefix â€œjust in case,â€ use user-agent sniffing to choose a prefix, or assume a prefix is harmless because the browser ignores unknown declarations. A prefix can change rendering, accessibility, or interaction behavior in only one engine.

```css
/* Avoid: a historical prefix pile with no support policy. */
/*
.box {
  -webkit-transform: translateZ(0);
  -moz-transform: translateZ(0);
  -ms-transform: translateZ(0);
  -o-transform: translateZ(0);
  transform: translateZ(0);
}
*/

/* Prefer the standard property when current targets support it. */
.box {
  transform: translateZ(0);
}
```

## Appendix E: Popular animation CSS and JavaScript libraries

Native CSS and the Web Animations API should be the first tools considered for straightforward transitions, keyframes, and progressive enhancements. Libraries become useful when a project needs reusable motion presets, timelines, springs, scroll coordination, SVG or canvas control, gesture handling, sequencing, or framework integration.

The right library is determined by the problem, not by how many effects its marketing page demonstrates. Evaluate bundle size, licensing, module format, accessibility guidance, cleanup behavior, server-side rendering support, and whether it respects reduced-motion preferences.

### CSS libraries and collections

#### Animate.css

[Animate.css](https://animate.style/) is a familiar collection of ready-made CSS keyframe animations. It is useful for quickly adding entrance, exit, attention, and emphasis effects without writing each `@keyframes` block yourself.

```html
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/animate.css@4/animate.min.css">

<h2 class="animate__animated animate__fadeInUp">
  A softly introduced heading
</h2>
```

Use a class-based library selectively. Importing a large catalog for one effect can add unnecessary CSS, and a class that automatically animates on page load can create motion for users who have requested less of it. Wrap the use in a reduced-motion policy when the library does not provide one globally.

```css
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .animate__animated {
    animation: none !important;
  }
}
```

#### Hover.css

[Hover.css](https://ianlunn.github.io/Hover/) is a collection of CSS transitions and hover effects for links, buttons, icons, and other interactive elements. Hover effects should have a keyboard equivalent: apply the same visual state to `:focus-visible` when the effect communicates interaction.

```html
<a class="button hvr-grow" href="/learn">Learn CSS</a>
```

```css
.hvr-grow:hover,
.hvr-grow:focus-visible {
  transform: scale(1.04);
}
```

#### Animista

[Animista](https://animista.net/) is a visual generator and collection of CSS animations. It is especially useful for exploring timing, transforms, and keyframes before copying a small, project-owned result into the stylesheet. Treat generated code as a starting point: rename keyframes, remove unused declarations, and add reduced-motion behavior.

#### Motion UI and component-system utilities

Design systems and component libraries often include motion tokens rather than a standalone animation library. A useful system defines durations, easing curves, distance scales, and reduced-motion alternatives as tokens.

```css
:root {
  --motion-duration-fast: 120ms;
  --motion-duration-standard: 220ms;
  --motion-ease-standard: cubic-bezier(.2, .8, .2, 1);
}

.popover {
  transition:
    opacity var(--motion-duration-fast) var(--motion-ease-standard),
    translate var(--motion-duration-standard) var(--motion-ease-standard);
}
```

The benefit is consistency and governance. A smaller set of tokens is easier to audit than hundreds of unrelated animation classes.

### JavaScript animation libraries

#### GSAP

[GSAP](https://gsap.com/docs/v3/) is a mature, framework-agnostic animation platform with tweens, timelines, easing, staggered animations, and optional plugins for scroll animation, dragging, motion paths, morphing, and more. It is a strong choice for complex choreography or projects that need precise sequencing and broad browser support.

```js
import { gsap } from 'gsap';

const context = gsap.context(() => {
  gsap.from('.card', {
    opacity: 0,
    y: 24,
    duration: 0.45,
    stagger: 0.08,
    ease: 'power2.out',
  });
});

// In a component teardown, revert the context to remove inline styles and listeners.
context.revert();
```

GSAP is powerful enough to become an application architecture. Use timelines for coordinated sequences, but keep semantic state in the DOM or application model rather than encoding state only in animation progress.

#### Motion

[Motion](https://motion.dev/) provides JavaScript, React, and Vue APIs for transforms, springs, gestures, scroll animations, sequences, and staggered effects. Its JavaScript API can animate HTML, SVG, and other values.

```js
import { animate, stagger } from 'motion';

animate(
  '.menu-item',
  { opacity: [0, 1], y: [12, 0] },
  { delay: stagger(0.06), duration: 0.3 }
);
```

For a scroll-linked effect, use the libraryâ€™s scroll API or native CSS scroll timelines where the browser support and behavior are sufficient. Avoid maintaining two independent sources of truth for the same effect.

```js
import { scroll } from 'motion';

const progress = document.querySelector('.progress');
if (progress) {
  scroll((progressValue) => {
    progress.style.transform = `scaleX(${progressValue})`;
  });
}
```

Add a reduced-motion guard and ensure the progress indicator has an accessible alternative, such as a native `<progress>` element or a text status.

#### anime.js

[anime.js](https://animejs.com/documentation/) is a lightweight animation engine for CSS properties, transforms, DOM and SVG attributes, JavaScript objects, keyframes, timelines, callbacks, and easing. It is a good fit for self-contained effects that do not need the full plugin ecosystem of a larger timeline platform.

```js
import anime from 'animejs';

anime({
  targets: '.dot',
  translateX: 180,
  rotate: '1turn',
  duration: 900,
  easing: 'easeOutElastic(1, .7)',
});
```

Check the version-specific API before copying examples. Major versions may change import paths and method signatures.

#### AOS (Animate On Scroll)

[AOS](https://michalsnik.github.io/aos/) applies data attributes to trigger predefined reveal animations as elements enter the viewport. It can be convenient for static marketing pages with simple entrance effects.

```html
<section data-aos="fade-up" data-aos-duration="500">
  <h2>Progressive enhancement</h2>
</section>
```

```js
import AOS from 'aos';
import 'aos/dist/aos.css';

AOS.init({
  once: true,
  disable: window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches,
});
```

For application interfaces with frequent DOM updates, inspect cleanup and mutation behavior carefully. An IntersectionObserver-based solution or native view timeline may be simpler.

#### ScrollReveal

[ScrollReveal](https://scrollrevealjs.org/) provides a small API for revealing elements as they enter the viewport. It is useful when the desired behavior is â€œanimate this group when it becomes visible,â€ rather than a continuous scroll-linked relationship.

```js
import ScrollReveal from 'scrollreveal';

const reduceMotion = window.matchMedia('(prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)').matches;

if (!reduceMotion) {
  ScrollReveal().reveal('.feature', {
    distance: '1rem',
    duration: 500,
    interval: 80,
    origin: 'bottom',
  });
}
```

#### Lottie

[Lottie](https://airbnb.io/lottie/) renders animations exported as JSON from motion-design tools. It is useful for illustrated status, onboarding, and brand motion when CSS shapes are not expressive enough. It is not a replacement for CSS transitions on ordinary controls.

```js
import lottie from 'lottie-web';

const animation = lottie.loadAnimation({
  container: document.querySelector('.empty-state__art'),
  renderer: 'svg',
  loop: false,
  autoplay: true,
  path: '/animations/empty-state.json',
});

// Stop or destroy it when the component leaves the page.
animation.addEventListener('complete', () => animation.pause());
```

Use a static image or a reduced-motion version when animation is not appropriate. Audit JSON size, SVG complexity, color contrast, and whether the animation communicates meaningful information.

### Choosing a library

Use this decision guide:

| Need | First option | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One hover or entrance effect | Native CSS | Smallest dependency and easiest progressive enhancement |
| A catalog of simple preset effects | Animate.css or Hover.css | Fast class-based setup |
| Visual experimentation before writing CSS | Animista | Generates editable CSS starting points |
| Complex sequences and timelines | GSAP | Mature timeline and plugin ecosystem |
| Springs, gestures, and framework motion | Motion | Modern APIs for JavaScript, React, and Vue |
| Lightweight CSS/SVG/object animation | anime.js | Compact API with broad target types |
| Simple viewport reveals | AOS or ScrollReveal | Declarative intersection-triggered effects |
| Designer-authored illustrations | Lottie | JSON-based motion assets |

### Library integration rules

1. Keep semantic state independent of animation progress.
2. Provide a no-library baseline that still exposes all content and controls.
3. Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` before initializing expensive effects.
4. Clean up observers, timelines, event listeners, and inline styles on teardown.
5. Reserve space for media and avoid layout shifts during animation setup.
6. Keep focus visible while elements move, fade, or scale.
7. Avoid animating large numbers of nodes when a parent transform or CSS timeline can express the same effect.
8. Pin dependency versions and read the current license and release documentation before shipping.

## Appendix F: Modern alternatives to `reset.css` and `normalize.css`

The current practical alternative is not always another giant reset file. Modern browsers agree on most of the old cross-browser inconsistencies, so many teams use a small, project-owned baseline inside a cascade layer, then add only the defaults their design system actually needs. This approach is sometimes called a sensible reset, a remedy, or a minimal baseline.

The choice depends on the project:

| Approach | What it does | Best fit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Minimal project-owned baseline | Changes only box sizing, typography inheritance, media defaults, and known application needs | Most custom applications and design systems |
| `normalize.css` | Preserves useful browser defaults while correcting documented inconsistencies | Broad cross-browser foundations and older target ranges |
| `sanitize.css` | Normalizes and adds opinionated sensible defaults | Teams that want a maintained foundation with more styling decisions |
| `modern-normalize` | Smaller normalization aimed at current Chrome, Firefox, and Safari behavior | Projects targeting evergreen browsers |
| Framework preflight | A framework-specific baseline, such as Tailwind Preflight or Bootstrap Reboot | Projects already committed to that framework |
| No global reset | Keeps user-agent defaults and styles components locally | Content-first pages, prototypes, and systems that value native defaults |

There is no universal â€œbestâ€ reset. The important decision is to choose one baseline, understand what it changes, and avoid stacking multiple resets that fight over the same elements.

### Recommended default: a layered, minimal baseline

For a new application, start with a small reset in a named layer. This keeps the baseline easy to inspect and prevents it from becoming an unowned collection of global overrides.

```css
@layer reset, base, components, utilities;

@layer reset {
  *,
  *::before,
  *::after {
    box-sizing: border-box;
  }

  html {
    text-size-adjust: 100%;
  }

  body {
    min-block-size: 100vh;
    margin: 0;
    line-height: 1.5;
    text-rendering: optimizeLegibility;
  }

  :where(h1, h2, h3, h4, p, figure, blockquote, dl, dd) {
    margin-block: 0;
  }

  :where(ul, ol)[role='list'] {
    padding: 0;
    list-style: none;
  }

  :where(img, picture, video, canvas, svg) {
    display: block;
    max-inline-size: 100%;
  }

  :where(input, button, textarea, select) {
    font: inherit;
  }

  :where(button, input, textarea, select) {
    color: inherit;
  }

  :where(textarea) {
    resize: vertical;
  }

  :where(button, label, select, summary) {
    cursor: pointer;
  }

  :where(button:disabled, input:disabled, select:disabled, textarea:disabled) {
    cursor: not-allowed;
  }
}
```

This baseline intentionally does not erase every browser default. Headings, lists, tables, buttons, and form controls still receive meaningful component or base styles instead of becoming blank boxes that every page must rebuild.

### Why use a cascade layer?

A reset is foundational CSS, so it should have a predictable relationship to the rest of the stylesheet. A reset layer can establish box sizing and baseline behavior while allowing components and utilities to override it normally.

```css
@layer reset, base, components, utilities;

@layer reset {
  [hidden] {
    display: none !important;
  }
}

@layer components {
  .dialog[open] {
    display: grid;
  }
}
```

The `[hidden]` rule is an example of a true boundary: an author component should not accidentally make a hidden element visible. Keep such exceptions rare and document them.

### Do not remove useful semantics

Older resets often removed all margins, list markers, outlines, button appearance, and form-control styling globally. Those declarations can save a designer from unexpected defaults, but they also remove useful affordances. A modern baseline should be selective.

```css
/* Risky as a global rule: it removes a valuable keyboard signal. */
/* *:focus { outline: none; } */

/* Better: keep a visible, branded focus indicator. */
:where(:focus-visible) {
  outline: 3px solid var(--color-accent, #1d4ed8);
  outline-offset: 3px;
}
```

Do not globally set `appearance: none` on every control. Do not remove list markers from every list when some lists are content. Do not make every image `user-select: none` unless the product has a specific interaction reason.

### Keep semantic lists semantic

Navigation lists and application menus often need visual list styles removed, but article lists and ordered procedures may need their markers. Scope the reset to the role or component that owns the visual treatment.

```css
/* Good: only presentation lists lose their markers. */
:where(ul, ol)[role='list'],
.nav-list,
.tag-list {
  padding: 0;
  list-style: none;
}

/* Keep this semantic list styled. */
.instructions {
  padding-inline-start: 1.5rem;
  list-style: decimal;
}
```

### Normalize instead of reset

If the project needs a cross-browser foundation that preserves useful defaults, use a maintained normalization package rather than combining several ad hoc snippets. [normalize.css](https://csstools.github.io/normalize.css/) is the conservative option: it targets browser inconsistencies while trying to keep elements recognizable. The current package documentation lists installation through `@csstools/normalize.css`.

```css
@import url('@csstools/normalize.css');

@layer base {
  /* Project-specific rules follow the normalization layer. */
  body {
    font-family: var(--font-reading);
  }
}
```

Treat normalization as a foundation, not a design system. You still need to define type, spacing, focus, form, and component behavior for the product.

### `sanitize.css`

[`sanitize.css`](https://csstools.github.io/sanitize.css/) is a more opinionated foundation that combines normalization with sensible defaults. It can be a good fit when a team wants a curated baseline across a broad set of elements.

```js
// JavaScript or TypeScript entry point
import 'sanitize.css';
```

Audit the package against the projectâ€™s accessibility requirements. A â€œsensibleâ€ default for one interface can be an unwanted global opinion for another, especially around form controls, media, typography, or print.

### `modern-normalize`

[`modern-normalize`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/modern-normalize) is a smaller normalization package aimed at current Chrome, Firefox, and Safari behavior. It can be appropriate for an evergreen-browser application that wants a compact starting point rather than broad legacy coverage.

```js
import 'modern-normalize/modern-normalize.css';
```

Check the packageâ€™s current target and maintenance status before adopting it. A smaller package is not automatically a better fit if the application must support browsers outside its documented scope.

### Framework preflights and reboots

Frameworks often include their own baseline. Tailwindâ€™s Preflight, Bootstrap Reboot, and UnoCSS reset presets are examples of framework-coupled approaches. Use the frameworkâ€™s baseline when the framework owns the rest of the styling model; avoid adding another global reset on top without comparing the output.

```css
/* Example: keep a framework baseline in its own layer. */
@import 'tailwindcss' layer(framework);
@layer framework, reset, base, components, utilities;
```

The exact import and layer behavior depends on the framework version. Read the current framework documentation and inspect the generated CSS rather than assuming that two reset layers compose safely.

### Component-local baselines

A design system can avoid a heavy global reset by making each component locally complete. This is especially useful for web components, embedded widgets, and applications that must coexist with host-page CSS.

```css
.date-picker {
  box-sizing: border-box;
  font: 1rem/1.4 system-ui, sans-serif;
}

.date-picker,
.date-picker::before,
.date-picker::after {
  box-sizing: inherit;
}

.date-picker button {
  font: inherit;
  color: inherit;
}
```

Component-local baselines reduce global side effects, but they require discipline. Put shared rules in a reusable layer or component primitive instead of copying a different mini-reset into every component.

### A reset decision workflow

1. List the browsers, embedded contexts, and rendering modes the product supports.
2. Decide whether user-agent defaults are useful for the content.
3. Choose one approach: minimal baseline, normalization package, sanitize-style foundation, framework preflight, or no reset.
4. Put the choice in a named layer and record it in the project documentation.
5. Test headings, lists, tables, forms, focus, media, `dialog`, print, forced colors, zoom, and reduced motion.
6. Remove rules that do not solve a demonstrated problem.
7. Recheck the baseline when changing browser targets or major framework versions.

### What this book uses

This bookâ€™s web edition uses a small project-owned baseline rather than importing a full reset package. It sets predictable box sizing, readable typography, media behavior, form inheritance, focus treatment, and responsive defaults in the application stylesheet. That approach keeps the visual contract close to the components and avoids silently changing native semantics across every element.

## Appendix G: A11y field guide

This appendix is a compact accessibility reference for CSS authors and component developers. â€œA11yâ€ is a short form of â€œaccessibilityâ€: the first and last letters of the word with the 11 letters between them. The abbreviation is useful, but the work is concrete: preserve semantics, make states perceivable, support multiple input methods, and test with people and tools.

### The four questions for every component

Before reviewing CSS, ask:

1. **Can I find it?** Is the component in a sensible reading and focus order?
2. **Can I understand it?** Does it have a clear name, role, state, value, and result?
3. **Can I operate it?** Can keyboard, touch, voice, switch, and assistive-technology users complete the task?
4. **Can I recover?** Are errors, focus changes, and unavailable enhancements explained and reversible?

### Semantic HTML first

Use the element that already expresses the intended behavior:

| Need | Prefer |
|---|---|
| Navigate somewhere | `<a href>` |
| Perform an action | `<button>` |
| Submit data | `<form>` and `<button type="submit">` |
| Expand content | `<details>` and `<summary>` |
| Modal decision | `<dialog>` |
| Choose one option | Radio group or `<select>` |
| Choose several options | Checkboxes |
| Progress toward a goal | `<progress>` |
| Measurement within a range | `<meter>` |
| Page regions | `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<aside>`, `<footer>` |

ARIA can describe a custom implementation, but it does not automatically supply keyboard behavior, focus management, validation, or state changes. The first rule of ARIA is to avoid adding it when native HTML already provides the required semantics.

### Focus and keyboard checklist

- Every interactive element is reachable with `Tab` or the component's documented arrow-key model.
- Focus is visible against every supported surface and in forced-colors mode.
- Focus is not moved unexpectedly during ordinary reading.
- Opening a dialog or menu moves focus to a logical destination.
- Closing an overlay returns focus to its trigger when possible.
- A keyboard user can escape a modal, popover, drawer, or menu.
- No element is keyboard-focusable while hidden or inert.
- Skip links or equivalent landmarks let users bypass repeated navigation.

```css
.skip-link {
  position: absolute;
  inset-inline-start: 1rem;
  inset-block-start: 1rem;
  transform: translateY(-200%);
  z-index: 10;
}

.skip-link:focus-visible {
  transform: none;
  padding: .7rem 1rem;
  background: #172033;
  color: #fff;
}
```

```html
<a class="skip-link" href="#main-content">Skip to main content</a>
<main id="main-content">...</main>
```

### A11y smoke test for a new component

Run this short test before opening a pull request:

1. Find the component without a mouse.
2. Operate its primary action with `Enter` and `Space` where appropriate.
3. Inspect the accessibility tree and confirm its name, role, and state.
4. Zoom to 200% and look for clipping or hidden controls.
5. Enable reduced motion and confirm that the task still works.
6. Enable forced colors or high contrast and confirm that state remains visible.
7. Replace sample text with a long translation.
8. Turn off JavaScript and confirm the baseline behavior.

### Common CSS failure patterns

| Failure | Why it harms users | Safer alternative |
|---|---|---|
| `outline: none` everywhere | Removes keyboard orientation | Use `:focus-visible` with a strong outline |
| Fixed height around text | Clips zoomed or translated content | Use `min-block-size` and natural height |
| `overflow: hidden` on articles | Hides content and focus targets | Use `overflow: clip` only when intentional, or allow flow |
| Color-only status | Excludes color-blind and forced-color users | Add text, icons, borders, or patterns |
| `pointer-events: none` on controls | Makes a control unreachable | Fix layering and hit areas instead |
| Reordered form fields | Creates a different reading sequence | Change the source order |
| Placeholder as a label | Disappears during input | Use a persistent `<label>` |
| Auto-playing motion | Can trigger discomfort and distraction | Pause, provide controls, respect reduced motion |
| Tiny touch targets | Makes activation difficult | Provide a generous hit area |
| Custom `div` controls | Missing keyboard and semantics | Start with native HTML |

### A11y test record

Keep a short record with each release. It should identify the page or component, the browsers and assistive technologies tested, the zoom and preference settings, discovered issues, severity, owner, and retest date. This turns accessibility from an informal hope into a repeatable quality practice.

```md
Accessibility test record

- Component or page:
- Release:
- Browser and version:
- Screen reader or accessibility tree tool:
- Keyboard path tested:
- Zoom/text-size setting:
- Reduced motion:
- Forced colors/high contrast:
- Touch or mobile device:
- Findings:
- Follow-up owner:
- Retest date:
```

### Severity and triage

Prioritize issues by user impact, not by how easy they are to fix. A missing keyboard path for a required task, inaccessible form error, or content hidden at zoom deserves urgent attention. A minor spacing inconsistency in a non-essential decorative region may wait.

When triaging, record the affected users, task, workaround if any, reproducibility, and whether the issue blocks completion. This gives product and engineering a shared basis for deciding what ships.
